newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Cocoa, coffee prices lose momentum after rise.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Cocoa, coffee prices lose momentum after rise.

text.p: Cocoa and coffee prices lost steam on Wednesday after touching fresh peaks earlier in the week.
Cocoa lurched lower, giving up some of the five-percent gain achieved the previous day on fears that output in the world's largest producer Ivory Coast would be less than expected.
London's May contract dipped below the 1,000 stg level, but finished off its lows at $1,006 stg per tonne, down four stg.

The supply situation was unclear after a report that conflicted with a statement on Tuesday by Ivorian Commodities Minister Guy-Alain Gauze that the country's 1996/97 crop would be less than one million tonnes.
Ivory Coast had sold 800,000 tonnes already and there would be no more to sell, said Gauze, attending talks of the International Cocoa Organization in London.
But industry sources and crop analysts in Ivory Coast told Reuters on Wednesday that 1996/97 cocoa arrivals were largely the same as last season when the country produced a record 1.2 million tonnes.
"The cocoa is there, unfortunately, so this year is not too different from last year," one source said.
Coffee also lost ground, showing little reaction to news that producers of lower quality robusta coffee seemed determined to cut supplies despite soaring prices.
Gauze said in London on Wednesday that a planned cut in exports of 1.3 million 60 kg bags for the first six months of 1997 would definitely be implemented.

The cuts were agreed in January by Ivory Coast, Africa's largest coffee producer, and the 13 other members of the Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC) to help narrow the huge price differential between robusta coffee and the premium arabica type of beans, grown mainly in Central and South America.
An ACPC meeting will be held next week to discuss the supply situation amid prices that have risen 50 percent this year.
But traders shugged off the statement by Gauze as prices slumped, exhausted by a prolonged rally.
"This means that the market does not believe (in the robusta export cuts) or it is not happening," said one European trader.
The May robusta contract in London finished $30 lower at $1,735 per tonne after Monday's rally, which was fuelled by retail price hikes.
White sugar also slipped after a bearish performance on the raw sugar market in New York dampened sentiment. May was down $1.10 at $305.70 in the late afternoon.
Metals prices ended the day mixed after a volatile day of trading left traders at a loss to gauge the market's mood.
"I haven't got a clue at the moment. Its been one of those days when it has been all over the place," one said.
Copper for delivery in three months on the London Metal Exchange failed to uncover sell stops under $2,330 and ended only $7 weaker at $2,338 per tonne.
Aluminium made another foray towards the $1,700 target before the rise was squashed by tumbling copper prices and the market finished down $9 at $1,666 per tonne.
Lead and zinc, however, were resilient, ending up $22 at $693 per tonne and up $24 at $1,275 per tonne respectively.
Gold prices closed in London $1.25 higher at $352.65 per ounce, still stuck in its $351-$355 range.

The rare precious metal palladium, however, led the complex, ending $2.00 weaker, but off its low on an unconfirmed report that major producer Russia could start exports to the world's largest consumer Japan this month.
Prices have shot up by about than $40 this year, partially on reports of reduced shipments from Russia, which accounts for 60 percent of world supplies.
Wheat prices in Chicago extended gains on talk that Egypt was seeking half a million tonnes of supplies and belief that soft red wheat acreage in the United States would fall.
Prices at mid-morning were two to 7-1/2 cents higher, with May up five cents at $3.87 per bushel.
Recent strong rallies in soybean prices led players to think wheat fields would be ploughed up and soybeans planted.

The prospect of more soybean supplies, however, rattled futures prices, which were mixed at midsession. Nearby contract months edged down amid a lack of investment fund buying, with May down three cents at $8.52-1/2 per bushel.
